title: Divine teaching stoops to the speech of the many
source_text: Εἰ νενόηται δὴ τὸ παράδειγμα. μεταβιβαστέον αὐτὸ ἐπὶ τὴν ποιότητα τῆς τῶν λογικῶν ζῴων λογικῆς τροφῆς. καὶ ὅρα εἰ μὴ Πλάτων μὲν καὶ οἱ Ἑλλήνων σοφοὶ ἐν οἷς λέγουσι καλῶς παραπλήσιοί εἰσι τοῖς προνοησαμένοις ἰατροῖς τῶν καθαριωτέρων εἶναι νομιζομένων μόνων, τοῦ πλήθους (δὲ) τῶν ἀνθρώπων καταφρονήσασιν· οἱ δ᾿ ἐν Ἰουδαίοις προφῆται καὶ οἱ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ μαθηταὶ, οἱ μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπόντες τῇ ποικίλῃ τῶν λέξεων συνθέσει καὶ τῇ, ὡς ὠνόμασεν ἡ γραφὴ, „σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων“ καὶ „σοφίᾳ“ „κατὰ σάρκα,“ τὴν γλῶσσαν αἰνισσομένη, ὁμοιωθεῖεν ἂν τοῖς τὴν αὐτὴν τῶν βρωμάτων ποιότητα ὑγιεινοτάτην προνοησαμένοις συνθέσει λέξεων σκευάσαι καὶ εὐτρεπίσαι φθανούσῃ ἐπὶ τὰ πλήθη τῶν ἀνθρώπων καὶ μὴ ξενιζούσῃ τὴν διάλεκτον αὐτῶν μηδὲ διὰ τοῦ ξενισμοῦ ἀποστρεφούσῃ ἀκούειν ὡς ἀσυνήθων τῶν τοιῶνδε διαλέξεων. καὶ γὰρ εἴπερ πρόκειται τῷ, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, λογικῷ βρώματι ἀνεξίκακον καὶ πρᾷον ποιῆσαι τὸν ἐμφαγόντα, πῶς οὐ βέλτιον συνεσκευασμένος εἴη ἂν λόγος ὁ πλήθη ἀνεξικάκων καὶ πρᾴων κατασκευάζων ἢ προκοπτόντων γε ἐπὶ ταύτας τὰς ἀρετὰς παρὰ τὸν πάνυ ὀλίγους καὶ εὐαριθμήτους, ἵνα (καὶ τοῦτο) δοθῇ, ἀνεξικάκους καὶ πρᾴους ποιοῦντα; ὥσπερ δὲ εἰ ὁ (Πλάτων) τοὺς αἰγυπτιάζοντας ἢ τοὺς συριάζοντας ὠφελεῖν ὑγιέσι δόγμασιν ἐβούλετο, Ἕλλην τυγχάνων, προενοήσατο ἂν μαθεῖν τὰς τῶν ἀκουσομένων διαλέκτους καὶ, ὡς Ἕλληνες ὀνομάζουσι, βαρβαρίζειν μᾶλλον ὑπὲρ τῆς Αἰγυπτίων καὶ Σύρων βελτιώσεως ἢ Ἕλλην μένων μηδὲν δύνασθαι χρήσιμον λέγειν Αἰγυπτίοις καὶ Σύροις· οὕτως ἡ προνοουμένη θεία φύσις οὐ τῶν πεπαιδεῦσθαι νομιζομένων μόνον τὰ Ἑλλήνων ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν Ἑλλήνων συγκατέβη τῇ ἰδιωτείᾳ τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἀκροωμένων, ἵνα ταῖς συνήθεσιν αὐτοῖς χρησαμένη λέξεσι προκαλέσηται ἐπὶ ἀκρόασιν τὸ τῶν ἰδιωτῶν πλῆθος, δυνάμενον ἐξ εὐχεροῦς μετὰ τὴν ἅπαξ γενομένην εἰσαγωγὴν φιλοτιμήσασθαι πρὸς τὸ καὶ βαθύτερα τῶν κεκρυμμένων νοημάτων ἐν ταῖς γραφαῖς καταλαβεῖν. καὶ τῷ τυχόντι γὰρ δῆλον, ταύτας ἀναγινώσκοντι, ὅτι πολλὰ βαθύτερον τοῦ αὐτόθεν ἐμφαινομένου ἔχειν δύναται νοῦν, τοῖς ἀνατιθεῖσιν αὑτοὺς τῇ ἐξετάσει τοῦ λόγου φανερούμενον. καὶ φανερούμενον> κατὰ τὴν ἀναλογίαν τῆς εἰς τὸν λόγον σχολῆς καὶ εἰς τὴν ἄσκησιν αὐτοῦ προθυμίας.
pass_a_gloss: If the example has been understood (νοέω), it must be transferred (μεταβιβαστέον) to the quality (ποιότης) of the rational food (λογικὴ τροφή) of rational living beings (λογικὰ ζῷα). And see whether Plato and the wise of the Greeks, in what they say well, are not like the physicians who provided for (προνοέω) only those thought cleaner, having despised (καταφρονέω) the multitude (πλῆθος) of men; but the prophets among the Jews and the disciples (μαθηταί) of Jesus, who said a long farewell (μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπόντες) to the varied (ποικίλη) composition (σύνθεσις) of words and to, as Scripture (γραφή) named it, 'wisdom of men' and 'wisdom' 'according to flesh' (κατὰ σάρκα), [Scripture] hinting at (αἰνίσσομαι) the tongue (γλῶσσα), would be likened (ὁμοιόω) to those who provided to prepare (σκευάζω) and make ready (εὐτρεπίζω) the same quality of foods most healthful in a composition of words reaching (φθάνω) to the multitudes of men and not making strange (ξενίζω) their dialect, nor through the strangeness (ξενισμός) turning them away (ἀποστρέφω) from hearing, as of unaccustomed (ἀσυνήθης) such discourses (διαλέξεις). For indeed if it is set before (πρόκειται) the, so that I may name it so, rational food (λογικὸν βρῶμα) to make forbearing (ἀνεξίκακος) and gentle (πρᾷος) the one eating, how would not better prepared be the discourse (λόγος) that builds (κατασκευάζω) multitudes of forbearing and gentle, or at least advancing (προκόπτω) to these virtues (ἀρεταί), than the one making very few and easily counted (εὐαρίθμητοι), so that this too be granted, forbearing and gentle? And as if Plato wished to benefit (ὠφελέω) those speaking Egyptian (αἰγυπτιάζω) or Syrian (συριάζω) with sound doctrines, being a Greek, he would have provided to learn the dialects of those who would hear, and, as Greeks name it, to barbarize (βαρβαρίζω) rather for the improvement (βελτίωσις) of Egyptians and Syrians than, remaining Greek, be able to say nothing useful to Egyptians and Syrians; so the providing divine nature (ἡ προνοουμένη θεία φύσις), not of those thought to be educated (παιδεύω) in Greek things only but also of the rest of the Greeks, came down together (συγκαταβαίνω) to the plainness (ἰδιωτεία) of the multitude of hearers, so that, using the words customary (συνήθεις) to them, it might summon (προκαλέομαι) to hearing the multitude of ordinary people (ἰδιῶται), able easily (ἐξ εὐχεροῦς), after the once-made introduction (εἰσαγωγή), to be ambitious (φιλοτιμέομαι) to grasp (καταλαμβάνω) even the deeper (βαθύτερα) of the hidden (κρύπτω) meanings (νοήματα) in the Scriptures. For it is plain even to the chance person (ὁ τυχών) reading them that many things can have a sense (νοῦς) deeper than what appears immediately (τὸ αὐτόθεν ἐμφαινόμενον), made manifest (φανερόω) to those who devote (ἀνατίθημι) themselves to the examination (ἐξέτασις) of the word (λόγος), <and made manifest> according to the proportion (ἀναλογία) of the leisure (σχολή) for the word and the eagerness (προθυμία) for its practice (ἄσκησις).
pass_b_english: If the example has been understood, we must carry it over to the quality of the rational food of rational beings. And consider whether Plato and the wise men of the Greeks, in the things they say well, are not like the physicians who cared only for those reckoned more refined and despised the multitude of men; while the prophets among the Jews and the disciples of Jesus, who would have nothing to do with the ornate arrangement of words, and with what Scripture has called “the wisdom of men” (1 Corinthians 2:5) and “wisdom according to the flesh” (compare 1 Corinthians 1:26; 2 Corinthians 1:12), phrases by which it hints at skill in language, might be likened to those who took care to prepare and make ready the same most wholesome quality of food in an arrangement of words that reaches the multitudes of men: one that does not sound foreign to their speech, and does not, by sounding foreign, turn them away from listening, as though such discourses were unfamiliar to them.

For indeed, if the aim of rational food, if I may call it so, is to make the one who eats it forbearing and gentle, how could the discourse that produces multitudes of forbearing and gentle people, or at least of people advancing towards these virtues, not be better prepared than the one that makes a very few, easily counted, forbearing and gentle, granting even that it does so?

And just as, if Plato, being a Greek, had wished to benefit with sound doctrines those who speak Egyptian or Syriac, he would have taken care to learn the languages of those who were to hear him, and, as the Greeks call it, to speak like a barbarian for the improvement of Egyptians and Syrians, rather than remain a Greek and be able to say nothing useful to Egyptians and Syrians; so the divine nature, which cares not only for those reckoned educated in Greek learning but also for the rest of the Greeks, came down to the plainness of the multitude of its hearers, so that, by using the words familiar to them, it might call the multitude of ordinary people to listen. Once they have been introduced, they can readily strive to grasp even the deeper of the meanings hidden in the Scriptures. For it is plain even to anyone at all who reads them that many passages can have a meaning deeper than what appears at first sight, a meaning that becomes clear to those who give themselves to examining the word, and becomes clear in proportion to the leisure they devote to the word and their zeal in its practice.

choices.choice: ‘The wisdom of men’ (σοφίᾳ ἀνθρώπων) is verbatim 1 Corinthians 2:5. ‘Wisdom according to the flesh’ is not verbatim in the New Testament: the nearest are 1 Corinthians 1:26 (σοφοὶ κατὰ σάρκα) and 2 Corinthians 1:12 (σοφίᾳ σαρκικῇ), cited with ‘compare’. The farewell to elaborate speech may also echo 1 Corinthians 2:1 and 2:4; left uncited as an allusion only. μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπόντες (literally ‘saying a long farewell to’): ‘would have nothing to do with’. τὴν γλῶσσαν αἰνισσομένη: Scripture by these phrases hints at ‘the tongue’, that is, at mere skill in language; rendered ‘hints at skill in language’. τῶν λοιπῶν Ἑλλήνων (‘the rest of the Greeks’) stands so in the staged text; one might expect ‘the rest of men’, but it is translated as printed. Koetschau’s supplements (δὲ), (Πλάτων) and (καὶ τοῦτο) accepted. ‘καὶ φανερούμενον>’ in the staged text is an HTML-escaped closing bracket of the editor’s supplement <καὶ φανερούμενον>; translated (‘and becomes clear’). ἀνεξίκακος ‘forbearing’, πρᾷος ‘gentle’. βαρβαρίζειν ‘to speak like a barbarian’ (to speak a non-Greek tongue). ἡ προνοουμένη θεία φύσις: ‘the divine nature, which cares for’, keeping πρόνοια language. τὸν λόγον: ‘the word’ in the sense of the Scriptures’ teaching, lowercase because not the personal Word.
μακρὰν χαίρειν εἰπόντες: archaic calque 'bade a long farewell to' -> 'would have nothing to do with'; ποικίλῃ 'elaborate' -> 'ornate'
Scripture phrases in Origen's voice put in double quotation marks, matching the other Book 7 chunks
τὴν γλῶσσαν αἰνισσομένη: 'hints at language' -> 'hints at skill in language'
'the same quality of food, most wholesome' -> 'the same most wholesome quality of food'; ξενιζούσῃ / ξενισμοῦ 'foreign' -> 'sound foreign'; ὡς ἀσυνήθων clause made natural

rhetorical question recast from Greek order: 'how could the discourse that produces multitudes of forbearing and gentle people ... not be better prepared'; πλήθη ... κατασκευάζων now 'produces multitudes of' (not 'makes multitudes')
1 Corinthians 2:5, 1:26 and 2 Corinthians 1:12 checked against the verses
